new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the last syllable of the word (gavró 'man', ḥozé 'he sees', ḥozyó 'she sees'; in the printed page the final syllables of the Mlaḥsô forms are set in boldface). Mlaḥsô retains the older Aramaic final stress that most other Eastern Neo-Aramaic languages have shifted to the penult. Independently confirmed by the same author in Jastrow [1986] JAAS 1: 13: 'word stress is on the last syllable'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Existence acknowledged but no placement rule: p. 350 says tense vowels are 'long to half-long in syllables carrying secondary stress'.
new_statements.exceptions: 'unless otherwise indicated' - deviations from the general rule are marked with an acute in the chapter; the proclitic definite article ə- 'occurs only in stressed non-final syllables' (ə́-gavro 'the man', ə́-brato 'the daughter'), i.e. the article carries the stress; the JAAS 1986 table shows qīmle 'he got up' (l-suffix preterite) apparently not final-stressed, though the scan's diacritics are not fully legible. Stress-group (phrase) reduction is stated for NENA generally, not specifically for Mlaḥsô.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress in citation and inflected forms (nouns and participle-based verb forms); comparative survey chapter written by the language's sole describer, so first-hand rather than second-hand.
new_statements.identity_note: The source describes Mlaḥsô proper (mlah1239; single village Mlaḥsô, Lice district, Diyarbakır province; data from survivors collected by Jastrow from 1968, later in Qamishli). No dialect split; Jastrow groups it with Ṭuroyo (turo1239) as Central/Western Eastern Neo-Aramaic but its final stress contrasts with Ṭuroyo's penultimate stress, so the two must not be conflated.
